Appendix A Correlator transformer: Detailed description

A major disadvantage of neural quantum states (NQS) is the limited understanding of their optimization and representation processes. Although we have techniques that minimize the energy or evolve the state in time (and so on), we have no intuition why certain parameters might be relevant or irrelevant.

To investigate this behavior, we employ a correlator transformer as an architecture for neural quantum states. The correlator transformer was introduced in Suresh et al. [43]. The model uses standard patched input configurations σi,p\sigma_{i,p} with a linear embedding:

Xi,m1=∑pσi,p​Wp,m​pEi,m,X1∈ℝ(Lx/p,Ly/p,2​p),X^{1}_{i,m}=\sum_{p}\sigma_{i,\mathrm{p}}\,W_{\mathrm{p},m}\,\mathrm{pE}_{i,m},\qquad X^{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{(L_{x}/p,L_{y}/p,2p)}, (56)

where ii indexes the patch, pp labels the position within a patch, and mm denotes the embedding dimension. Here, Wp,mW_{\mathrm{p},m} are trainable network parameters and pEi,m\mathrm{pE}_{i,m} represents the standard positional encoding:

pEi,m={sin⁡(i100002​j/d)m=2​j,cos⁡(i100002​j/d)m=2​j+1.\mathrm{pE}_{i,m}=\left\{\begin{matrix}\sin\left(\frac{i}{10000^{2j/d}}\right)&m=2j,\\ \cos\left(\frac{i}{10000^{2j/d}}\right)&m=2j+1.\end{matrix}\right. (57)

The matrix Xi,m1X^{1}_{i,m} that contains first order correlations is then used to calculate the query QnQ_{n} and key KnK_{n} values of the transformer:

Qn=X1​Wn​QandKn=Xn​Wn​K,Q_{n}=X^{1}W^{nQ}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad K_{n}=X^{n}W^{nK}, (58)

the value matrix, on the other hand, is given by: Vn=pE​Wn​VV_{n}=\mathrm{pE}W^{nV} where Wn​QW^{nQ}, Wn​KW^{nK} and Wn​VW^{nV} are network weights. A product of query, key, and value matrices defines the output of the corresponding layer:

Xn+1=12​p​Qn​KnT​Vn.X^{n+1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2p}}Q_{n}K_{n}^{T}V_{n}. (59)

All outputs 𝕏=[X¯1,X¯2,…,X¯i,…,X¯n]\mathbb{X}=[\bar{X}^{1},\bar{X}^{2},\dots,\bar{X}^{i},\dots,\bar{X}^{n}], with X¯i=mean⁡(Xi)\bar{X}^{i}=\mathrm{mean}(X^{i}) are then used in a linear layer, with weights WpredW^{\mathrm{pred}}, to predict the probability of the corresponding input configuration:

ψ⁡(σ→)=Wpred​𝕏​(σ→)+β.\psi(\vec{\sigma})=W^{\mathrm{pred}}\mathbb{X}(\vec{\sigma})+\beta. (60)

This wave function of polynomial form allows us to interpret the processes within the transformer. Here, we included the bias β\beta as this corresponds to 0th0^{\mathrm{th}} order correlations.

Number of parameters.— To ensure a fair comparison between different correlation orders, we keep the total number of trainable parameters approximately constant. The total number of parameters depends on the system size (Nx×NyN_{x}\times N_{y}), the patch size psizep_{\mathrm{size}}, and the embedding dimension edime_{\mathrm{dim}}.

The equation that defines the number of parameters is given by:

#​params=(psize​edim⏟embedding+Nx​Nypsize​edim⏟pE)+3​(nlay−1)​edim2⏟decoder+nlay+1⏟Wpred+β\displaystyle\begin{split}\#\mathrm{params}=(\underbrace{p_{\mathrm{size}}e_{\mathrm{dim}}}_{\mathrm{embedding}}+\underbrace{\frac{N_{x}N_{y}}{p_{\mathrm{size}}}e_{\mathrm{dim}}}_{\mathrm{\mathrm{pE}}})\\ +~\underbrace{3(n_{\mathrm{lay}}-1)e_{\mathrm{dim}}^{2}}_{\mathrm{decoder}}+\underbrace{n_{\mathrm{lay}}+1}_{W^{\mathrm{pred}}+\beta}\end{split} (61)

Optimization.— To optimize the NQS, we use standard stochastic reconfiguration techniques [9] (with a learning rate of α=0.01\alpha=0.01) provided by the NetKet package [66].

Appendix B Generalizing to other encodings and non-spin systems

In the main text we focused our analysis on spin-1/21/2 systems. However, the idea to expand systems in terms of monomials of the input can be extended to systems with one-hot encoding or to cases with higher local Hilbert space dimensions.

One-hot encoding.— We start by discussing one-hot encoding for general systems. This method embeds the Hilbert space of the system in a much larger one and truncates it afterward. To provide an intuitive example, we stick to a system with {−1,1}L\{-1,1\}^{L} spins. When using one-hot encoding, the effective Hilbert space is given by: {{0,1},{0,1}}L\{\{0,1\},\{0,1\}\}^{L}. Since we are not interested in the whole effective Hilbert space, we truncate it and use the decision tree formalism. The indicator polynomial of the extended local Hilbert space is given by:

𝟙α,β​(σs)=𝟙α​(σ1s)​𝟙β​(σ2s)=∑α,β∈{0,1}L1−4​(α−12)​(σ1s−12)2​1−4​(β−12)​(σ2s−12)2,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\mathbb{1}_{\alpha,\beta}(\sigma^{s})=\mathbb{1}_{\alpha}(\sigma^{s}_{1})\mathbb{1}_{\beta}(\sigma^{s}_{2})=\\ &\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1\}^{L}}\frac{1-4(\alpha-\frac{1}{2})(\sigma^{s}_{1}-\frac{1}{2})}{2}\frac{1-4(\beta-\frac{1}{2})(\sigma^{s}_{2}-\frac{1}{2})}{2},\end{split} (62)

which reduces to:

𝟙α/β(σ1/2s)={σ1/2sfor​α/β=1,1−σ1/2sfor​α/β=0.\mathbb{1}_{\alpha/\beta}(\sigma^{s}_{1/2})=\left\{\begin{matrix}\sigma^{s}_{1/2}&\mathrm{for~}\alpha/\beta=1,\\ 1-\sigma^{s}_{1/2}&\mathrm{for~}\alpha/\beta=0.\end{matrix}\right. (63)

This produces a polynomial similar to Eq. (12) (considering that σ1s=1−σ2s\sigma^{s}_{1}=1-\sigma^{s}_{2}). Hence, one hot encoding does not offer an immediate advantage (or disadvantage) compared to typical spin encoding. Note that the monomials are no longer orthogonal. Nevertheless, this expression can be useful, as it allows a relatively simple understanding of how it groups states: Terms of degree kk contribute to the coefficient of 2L−k2^{L-k} basis states. Therefore, characterizing a basis state requires one system size order correlation. E.g. a product state of up spins is given by ψ↑​(σ→)=∏i=1Lσ2,i\psi_{\uparrow}(\vec{\sigma})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}\sigma_{2,i}, whereas down spins are given by ψ↓​(σ→)=∏i=1Lσ1,i\psi_{\downarrow}(\vec{\sigma})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}\sigma_{1,i}.

Non binary local Hilbert space dimension.— Finally, we turn to systems with larger local Hilbert spaces and non binary encoding. To do so, we introduce the Lagrange basis, a more general form of the indicator polynomial [67, 68, 69]. It defines an orthonormal basis {l1​(xs),l2​(xs),…,lk​(xs)}\{l_{1}(x^{s}),l_{2}(x^{s}),...,l_{k}(x^{s})\} at site ss for a local Hilbert space dimension {x1s,x2s,…,xks}\{x^{s}_{1},x^{s}_{2},...,x^{s}_{k}\} of kk. The polynomial lαs​(xs)l_{\alpha^{s}}(x^{s}) is defined by:

lαjs(xs)=∏0≤m≤km≠jxs−αmsαjs−αms={1for​xs=αs,0else.l_{\alpha^{s}_{j}}(x^{s})=\prod_{\underset{m\neq j}{0\leq m\leq k}}\frac{x^{s}-\alpha^{s}_{m}}{\alpha_{j}^{s}-\alpha^{s}_{m}}=\left\{\begin{matrix}1&\mathrm{for~}x^{s}=\alpha^{s},\\ 0&\mathrm{else.}\end{matrix}\right. (64)

with xs,αjs∈{x1s,x2s,…,xks}x^{s},\alpha^{s}_{j}\in\{x^{s}_{1},x^{s}_{2},...,x^{s}_{k}\}. The complete orthonormal basis for all sites SS is then defined by:

Lα→​(x→)=∏s∈Slαs​(xs),L_{\vec{\alpha}}(\vec{x})=\prod_{s\in S}l_{\alpha^{s}}(x^{s}), (65)

which allows us to write the wave function as:

ψ⁡(x→)=∑α→∈{x1,…,xk}nψ⁡(α→)​Lα→​(x→).\psi(\vec{x})=\sum_{\vec{\alpha}\in\{x_{1},...,x_{k}\}^{n}}\psi(\vec{\alpha})L_{\vec{\alpha}}(\vec{x}). (66)

Thus, the resulting wave function is a polynomial of degree (k−1)×n(k-1)\times n. Although the analysis in this regime becomes more challenging, as the maximal polynomial order grows much faster with system size and its monomials are no longer orthogonal, we can still conclude that even for simple product states high expansion orders are required.

Appendix C Spanning tree formalism applied to the toric code model restricted to the physical sector

Studying the perturbed toric code model is a difficult task as the Hilbert space grows with 22​(Lx×Ly)2^{2(L_{x}\times L_{y})}. However, restricting the analysis to the physical sector, where Gauss’s law is always fulfilled, reduces the effective Hilbert space dimension to 2Lx×Ly+12^{L_{x}\times L_{y}+1}. Following the spanning tree formalism allows us to limit the number of relevant spins to Lx×Ly+1L_{x}\times L_{y}+1 [70, 46, 71]. This is shown in Fig. 6. Spins on the red links determine the full configuration and span the complete orthogonal basis (according to Eq. (14)). Consequently, the remaining Lx×Ly−1L_{x}\times L_{y}-1 spins on the black links are linearly dependent on the “basis spins” and thus contain relevant information about potentially higher-order correlations of the Lx×Ly+1L_{x}\times L_{y}+1 basis spins.

Note that the spanning tree shown in Fig. 6 is not unique: translations and rotations of this tree will yield an equally well-suited orthogonal basis.

Appendix D Relation between ψ⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma), p⁡(σ)p(\sigma), and log⁡ψ⁡(σ)\log\psi(\sigma)

In this section, we clarify the relationship between three representations of a quantum state that appear naturally in the literature: ψ⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma), p⁡(σ)=|ψ|2p(\sigma)=|\psi|^{2}, and log⁡ψ⁡(σ)\log\psi(\sigma). Although related, these objects have generally different Fourier structures.

D.1 Probability and spin-moments

The probability distribution of a quantum many body state is given by the square of the wave function p⁡(σ)=|ψ⁡(σ)|2p(\sigma)=|\psi(\sigma)|^{2} and therefore describe similar things. In particular, in some autoregressive neural quantum states, the network output directly parametrizes p⁡(σ)p(\sigma), which raises the question how both are related from a boolean function point of view. The Fourier coefficients p¯​(S)\bar{p}(S) of the probability p⁡(σ)=∑S⊆[L]p¯​(S)​𝒳S​(σ)p(\sigma)=\sum_{S\subseteq[L]}\bar{p}(S)\mathcal{X}_{S}(\sigma) are given by:

p¯​(S)=12L​∑σψ∗​(σ)​ψ​(σ)​χs​(σ)=12L​∑σ∑S′,S′′ψ¯∗​(S′)​ψ¯​(S′′)​χs​(σ)​χs′​(σ)​χs′′​(σ).\begin{split}\bar{p}(S)&=\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\psi^{*}(\sigma)\psi(\sigma)\chi_{s}(\sigma)\\ &=\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{S^{\prime},S^{\prime\prime}}\bar{\psi}^{*}(S^{\prime})\bar{\psi}(S^{\prime\prime})\chi_{s}(\sigma)\chi_{s^{\prime}}(\sigma)\chi_{s^{\prime\prime}}(\sigma).\end{split} (67)

Using χA​(σ)​χA+B​(σ)=χB​(σ)\chi_{A}(\sigma)\chi_{A+B}(\sigma)=\chi_{B}(\sigma) and 12L​∑σχA​(σ)​χB​(σ)=δA,B\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\chi_{A}(\sigma)\chi_{B}(\sigma)=\delta_{A,B}, this equation reduces to:

p¯​(S)=12L​∑σ∑S′,δψ¯∗​(S′)​ψ¯​(S′​Δ​δ)​χs​(σ)​χδ​(σ)=∑S′⊆[L]ψ¯∗​(S′)​ψ¯​(S​Δ​S′),\begin{split}\bar{p}(S)&=\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{S^{\prime},\delta}\bar{\psi}^{*}(S^{\prime})\bar{\psi}(S^{\prime}\Delta\delta)\chi_{s}(\sigma)\chi_{\delta}(\sigma)\\ &=\sum_{S^{\prime}\subseteq[L]}\bar{\psi}^{*}(S^{\prime})\bar{\psi}(S\Delta S^{\prime}),\end{split} (68)

where Δ\Delta denotes the difference between sets. Consequently, the Fourier coefficients p¯​(S)\bar{p}(S) is defined as a convolution of the (ψ¯∗∗ψ¯)​(S)=∑S′⊆[L]ψ¯∗​(S′)​ψ¯​(S​Δ​S′)(\bar{\psi}^{*}*\bar{\psi})(S)=\sum_{S^{\prime}\subseteq[L]}\bar{\psi}^{*}(S^{\prime})\bar{\psi}(S\Delta S^{\prime}). Thus, although there exists a clear relation between p⁡(σ)p(\sigma) and ψ⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma), their Fourier coefficients may differ significantly from one another.

Remark.— The Fourier coefficients p¯​(S)\bar{p}(S) can be identified as spin moments ⟨∏i∈Sσ^iz⟩=12L​∑σψ∗​(σ)​ψ​(σ)​χs​(σ)\langle\prod_{i\in S}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i}\rangle=\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\psi^{*}(\sigma)\psi(\sigma)\chi_{s}(\sigma) and therefore have a direct physical interpretation.

D.2 Logarithmic parametrization of the neural quantum states

In practice, neural quantum states are often defined by using log⁡ψ⁡(σ)=f⁡(σ)\log\psi(\sigma)=f(\sigma) instead of ψ⁡(σ)=f⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma)=f(\sigma), where f⁡(σ)f(\sigma) is the neural network implementation. This trick is often applied to gain numerical stability, as ψ⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma) can vary over many orders of magnitude, which is related to requiring large correlation orders. Although, the logarithmic implementation can be understood as adding another activation function, the question arises, how their expansion coefficients f¯​(S)\bar{f}(S) and ψ¯​(S)\bar{\psi}(S) are related:

ψ¯​(S)=12L​∑σexp⁡(f⁡(σ))​𝒳S​(σ)=12L​∑σ(∑n=0∞1n!​f​(σ)n)​𝒳S​(σ)=∑n=0∞1n!​∑S1,…,Sn⊆[L]f¯​(S1)​…​f¯​(Sn)12L​∑σ𝒳S1​(σ)​…​𝒳Sn​(σ)​𝒳S​(σ)⏟δSn,S​Δ​S1​Δ​…​Δ​Sn−1=∑n=0∞1n!​∑S1,…,Sn−1⊆[L]f¯​(S1)​…f¯​(Sn−1)​f¯​(S​Δ​S1​Δ​…​Δ​Sn−1)=∑n=0∞1n!​f¯∗n​(S).\begin{split}\bar{\psi}(S)=&\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\exp(f(\sigma))\mathcal{X}_{S}(\sigma)\\ =&\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}f(\sigma)^{n}\right)\mathcal{X}_{S}(\sigma)\\ =&\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{S_{1},...,S_{n}\subseteq[L]}\bar{f}(S_{1})...\bar{f}(S_{n})\\ &\underbrace{\frac{1}{2^{L}}\sum_{\sigma}\mathcal{X}_{S_{1}}(\sigma)...\mathcal{X}_{S_{n}}(\sigma)\mathcal{X}_{S}(\sigma)}_{\delta_{S_{n},S\Delta S_{1}\Delta...\Delta S_{n-1}}}\\ =&\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{S_{1},...,S_{n-1}\subseteq[L]}\bar{f}(S_{1})...\\ &\bar{f}(S_{n-1})\bar{f}(S\Delta S_{1}\Delta...\Delta S_{n-1})\\ =&\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\bar{f}^{*n}(S).\end{split} (69)

Therefore, ψ¯​(S)\bar{\psi}(S) is a sum of all possible nn-fold convolutions f¯∗n​(S)\bar{f}^{*n}(S). Consequently, even if high expansion orders of ψ⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma) are required, a finite expansion order of f⁡(σ)f(\sigma) can be sufficient, if the magnitude of the low expansion order coefficients f¯​(S)\bar{f}(S) is large enough.

Remark.— Due to ψ⁡(σ)=exp⁡(fA+fB+fA​B)=exp⁡(fA)​exp⁡(fB)​exp⁡(fA​B)\psi(\sigma)=\exp(f_{A}+f_B+f_{AB})=\exp(f_A)\exp(f_B)\exp(f_{AB}), with fr=∑S⊆rf¯​(S)​𝒳S​(σS)f_{r}=\sum_{S\subseteq r}\bar{f}(S)\mathcal{X}_{S}(\sigma_{S}) only coefficients f¯​(SA∪SB)\bar{f}(S_{A}\cup S_{B}) with SA,SB≠∅S_{A},S_{B}\neq\emptyset can contribute to the entanglement between subsystem AA and BB of the quantum state.

Appendix E Deriving entanglement bounds

In this section, we derive the entanglement scalings for an NQS that contains expansion orders up to order n≤1/2​Xn\leq 1/2X, with X being the smaller bipartition of a system. The binary entropy approximation is given by [55, 56]:

Sbound​(n,X)=−n​ln⁡(nX)−(X−n)​ln⁡(1−nX).S_{\mathrm{bound}}(n,X)=-n\ln\left(\frac{n}{X}\right)-(X-n)\ln\left(1-\frac{n}{X}\right). (70)

Of interest are the three distinct regimes: constant expansion order, area law scaling, and volume law scaling.

Constant expansion order nn.— In the large XX regime, a constant expansion order nn yields maximally logarithmic entanglement growth:

Sbound​(n,X)=−n​ln⁡(nX)⏟∝n​ln⁡(X)−(X−n)​ln⁡(1−nX)⏟∝n.S_{\mathrm{bound}}(n,X)=\underbrace{-n\ln\left(\frac{n}{X}\right)}_{\propto n\ln(X)}-\underbrace{(X-n)\ln\left(1-\frac{n}{X}\right)}_{\propto n}. (71)

States with area law entanglement.— To simplify the derivation, we use the Ansatz n=X​f​(X)n=\sqrt{X}f(X):

Sbound​(n,X)/X=c=f⁡(x)​ln⁡(Xf⁡(X))−(X−f⁡(X))​ln⁡(1−f⁡(X)X)⏟≈f⁡(X)≪X−f⁡(X)X.\begin{split}&S_{\mathrm{bound}}(n,X)/\sqrt{X}=c\\ &=f(x)\ln\left(\frac{\sqrt{X}}{f(X)}\right)-(\sqrt{X}-f(X))\underbrace{\ln\left(1-\frac{f(X)}{\sqrt{X}}\right)}_{\overset{f(X)\ll\sqrt{X}}{\approx}-\frac{f(X)}{\sqrt{X}}}.\end{split} (72)

In the case f⁡(x)=c​o​n​s​t.f(x)=const. and f⁡(X)≪Xf(X)\ll\sqrt{X}, we get a scaling of Sbound∝X​ln⁡(X)S_{\mathrm{bound}}\propto\sqrt{X}\ln\left(X\right). Therefore, we can assume ∂Xf⁡(X)<0\partial_{X}f(X)<0 and f⁡(X)≪xf(X)\ll\sqrt{x} in the large X limit. With these assumptions, the above equation reduces to:

c≈f⁡(X)​(ln⁡(X)−ln⁡(f⁡(X)))−(f⁡(X)−f2​(X)X)⏟⟶0.c\approx f(X)\left(\ln\left(\sqrt{X}\right)-\ln\left(f(X)\right)\right)-\underbrace{(f(X)-\frac{f^{2}(X)}{\sqrt{X}})}_{\longrightarrow 0}. (73)

This leaves us with three cases to consider:

  • •

    f⁡(X)∝1ln⁡(X)f(X)\propto\frac{1}{\ln(X)}: this cancels the scaling of ln⁡X\ln\sqrt{X} and −ln⁡(f⁡(X))∝ln⁡(X)-\ln(f(X))\propto\ln(X) and therefore solves the equation.

  • •

    f⁡(X)f(X) decays faster than 1ln⁡(X)\frac{1}{\ln(X)}: f⁡(X)​ln⁡(f⁡(X))f(X)\ln\left(f(X)\right) becomes the leading term, but decays to zero.

  • •

    f⁡(X)f(X) decays slower than 1ln⁡(X)\frac{1}{\ln(X)}: the leading term f⁡(X)​ln⁡(X)f(X)\ln\left(\sqrt{X}\right) increases in magnitude with X. This includes more than pure area law scaling.

Consequently, CQS need a correlation scaling of n∝Xln⁡(X)n\propto\frac{\sqrt{X}}{\ln(X)} to be able to represent states with area law entanglement.

States with volume law entanglement.— We start again with n=X​f​(X)n=Xf(X):

c=−f⁡(X)​ln⁡(f⁡(X))−(1−f⁡(X))​ln⁡(1−f⁡(X)),c=-f(X)\ln\left(f(X)\right)-(1-f(X))\ln\left(1-f(X)\right), (74)

which is the binary entropy function H⁡(f⁡(X))=cH(f(X))=c. The solution f​(X)=H−1​(c)f(X)=H^{-1}(c) has one valid, X independent solution for f⁡(X)≤1/2f(X)\leq 1/2 (the regime where our approximation holds). Thus, n has to scale with the volume XX to obtain volume law entanglement scaling.

Instructions for reporting errors
